posts.title: Is someone already inside your phone?
posts.listDesc: The 5-minute check that tells you for sure — session lists, unknown devices, and what to do if you find something.
posts.intro: Not a hypothetical — an actual 5-minute check you can run right now, on the exact phone you're reading this on. No apps to install, nothing to buy.
posts.statLine: $ context — 292 days is the average time it takes someone to notice their login was stolen (IBM). Most people never check until something's already gone wrong.

paragraphs: Go to Settings → [your name] → Password Options → Security Recommendations, or check Settings → [your name] and scroll to see every device signed into your Apple ID.
Open the Google app → Profile picture → Manage your Google Account → Security → Your devices. This lists every device currently signed into your Google account.
Look for anything you don't recognize — a device model you've never owned, a city you've never been to, or a login time you can't account for.

sections.title: Look for apps you didn't install

paragraphs: Scroll through your full app list (not just your home screen — the full list in Settings → Apps). Stalkerware and spyware apps are often disguised with generic names like "System Update," "Device Health," or "Battery Optimizer."
If you don't remember installing it and can't explain what it does, that's worth investigating before you dismiss it.

sections.title: Check for a profile you didn't set up

paragraphs: Go to Settings → General → VPN & Device Management. If you see a configuration profile you didn't install yourself, someone else may have remote access to your device. This is a legitimate red flag, not routine.
Go to Settings → Security → Device admin apps. Anything listed here that you didn't knowingly enable (like a "Find My Device" app you don't recognize) deserves a closer look.

sections.title: Run your phone's built-in security checkup

paragraphs: Both Google and Apple have a one-tap privacy checkup built in — Google Account → Security → Security Checkup, or on iPhone, review the Security Recommendations screen from Step 1. These flag weak or reused passwords and unfamiliar sign-ins automatically.

quiz.question: Have you checked which devices are logged into your phone or accounts in the last 6 months?

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU FIND SOMETHING
warn.text: Don't panic, but do act. Sign out of any device you don't recognize immediately, change your password from a device you trust (not the compromised one), and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't already on. If it looks like stalkerware specifically, consider that removing it may alert whoever installed it — if this is a safety concern involving another person, that's worth thinking through carefully before you act.

checklist: Checked which devices are logged into your Apple ID / Google account
Scanned your full app list for anything unfamiliar
Checked for configuration profiles / device admin apps you didn't set up

posts.title: The password mistake nobody thinks is a big deal
posts.listDesc: Why reusing one password anywhere is worse than you think, and how a password manager actually fixes it.
posts.intro: Spoiler: it's using the same password in more than one place. It feels harmless. It's actually the single biggest reason accounts get taken over.
posts.statLine: $ context — one leaked password from any site you've ever used can unlock every other account where you reused it. This is called credential stuffing, and it's mostly automated.

sections.title: See if you've actually done this

paragraphs: Go to passwords.google.com or Settings → Password Manager → Password Checkup. It will show you exactly which passwords are reused, weak, or found in a known breach.
Go to Settings → Passwords → Security Recommendations. It flags reused and compromised passwords the same way.
Most people are surprised by how many show up — this is normal, not a sign you did something unusually careless.

bad.label: ✕ ONE PASSWORD, EVERYWHERE
bad.text: One site gets breached. Your email + password combo leaks. Automated tools try that exact combo on hundreds of other sites — banking, email, social media — in seconds.

good.label: ✓ UNIQUE PER SITE
good.text: One site gets breached. That leaked password is useless everywhere else, because it was never used anywhere else. The damage stays contained to one account.

sections.title: Set up a password manager (it's easier than remembering)

paragraphs: You don't need to memorize unique passwords — a password manager does. Your phone almost certainly already has one built in and free: iCloud Keychain on iPhone, or Google Password Manager on Android/Chrome.
If you want something that works the same across every device and browser regardless of platform, Bitwarden is free and widely trusted. Either option is a real upgrade from memorizing passwords.

sections.title: Fix your most important accounts first

paragraphs: You don't need to fix everything today. Start with the accounts that would hurt most if compromised: your primary email (it can reset almost everything else), your banking apps, and any account with saved payment info.
Let the password manager generate a new, unique password for each one as you go.

warn.label: ⚠ IF A PASSWORD SHOWS UP AS "COMPROMISED"
warn.text: Change it immediately, starting with that account and anywhere else you used the same one. If it's your email password specifically, treat it as urgent — email is usually the master key to everything else you own online.

checklist: Ran a password checkup to see what's reused or compromised
Turned on your phone's built-in password manager
Fixed email, banking, and payment-linked accounts first
Let the manager generate unique passwords going forward

posts.title: What is smishing?
posts.listDesc: The exact texts scammers send, why they work, and how to tell a real message from a fake one in seconds.
posts.intro: SMS phishing — a scam text designed to look official enough that you click without thinking. Here's the pattern behind almost every one you'll ever get.
posts.statLine: $ context — smishing works because texts feel more urgent and more "official" than email, and most people have never been taught to question one.

sections.title: The pattern, not the exact words

paragraphs: Almost every smishing text follows the same structure: a trusted name (your bank, a delivery company, the tax office), a problem that needs fixing right now, and a link to "fix" it. The specific wording changes constantly — the structure almost never does.

items.text: Claims a package couldn't be delivered and needs a small fee or address confirmation via a link.
Claims suspicious activity on your account and asks you to "verify" by logging in through their link.
Claims you've won something and just need to "claim" it before a countdown ends.

sections.title: Check the sender, not just the message

paragraphs: Real companies text from consistent, verifiable numbers or short codes. Scam texts often come from a random-looking mobile number, an email-style address, or a number that changes every time.
If in doubt, check your past messages from that company — does the number match what you've seen before?

sections.title: Never tap the link — go direct instead

paragraphs: Don't tap the link in the text, even to "just look." Instead, open the company's official app directly, or type their known website address yourself. If something's actually wrong with your account or delivery, it'll show up there too.

sections.title: Notice the urgency — it's the biggest tell

paragraphs: "Act now," "your account will be suspended," "offer expires in 1 hour" — manufactured urgency is doing the scammer's work for them. It's designed to make you click before you think. Real companies rarely demand instant action over text.

quiz.question: When you get a text claiming there's a "delivery problem," what do you do?
quiz.safeLabel: Check the official app or site instead

warn.label: ⚠ IF YOU'VE ALREADY CLICKED
warn.text: Don't enter anything if a page asks for a password, card number, or OTP — close it immediately. If you already entered something, change that password right away and check your bank/card statements for anything unfamiliar over the next few days.

checklist: Checked whether the sender number matches past legitimate messages
Didn't tap the link — went to the official app/site directly instead
Noticed the manufactured urgency for what it was
Knows what to do if a link was already tapped
